caption:
Baby in a sling? Tip your head forward. You should be able to kiss the top of their head.

WHY: a baby who sits too low, in loose fabric, can slump down, and that can make it harder for them to breathe. High and snug stops them slumping and keeps their face where you can see it. It's the C in the T.I.C.K.S. sling checklist the NHS and The Lullaby Trust share.

THE KISS CHECK (every time you put the sling on):
1. Tip your head forward. Can you kiss their head or forehead?
2. Can't reach? Tighten the sling and lift them higher, so they're hugged close against you.
3. Glance down: you should see their face without moving any fabric.

THE CATCH: never let the material cover their head, and don't feed a baby while they're in the sling (The Lullaby Trust says this is especially true under 4 months). Follow your sling's own instructions.

Do this: tip your head, kiss their head.

Send this to a friend who just got a sling.

Part 2 tomorrow, 7 pm: the chin check.

Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.

General information only, not medical advice.

caption:
Baby in a sling? You should always be able to slide one finger under their chin.

WHY: a baby curled so their chin is forced onto their chest can find it harder to breathe. NHS guidance says keep their chin off their chest, with at least a finger's width of space under it. It's the K in the T.I.C.K.S. sling checklist.

THE CHIN CHECK:
1. Slide one finger under their chin. It should fit.
2. Chin pressed down? Gently reposition them so their chin lifts off their chest.
3. Check the back: snug and upright, tummy and chest against you, not slumped low.

Part 1 was the kiss check: tip your head forward and you should be able to kiss their head.

THE CATCH: never let fabric cover their head, and don't feed a baby in the sling (especially under 4 months). Follow your sling's own instructions.

Do this: slide one finger under their chin.

Send this to whoever does the sling walks.

Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.

General information only, not medical advice.
